- The pseudocode below adds the numbers 1 to 3

| Count | Total | OUTPUT |
|---|---|---|
|   | 0 |   |
| 1 | 1 |   |
| 2 | 3 |   |
| 3 | 6 |   |
|   |   | 6 |

- The first row holds the initial value of `Total`; `Count` has no value yet
- **Never add a row for a FOR loop counter going past its end value**: the loop stops after `Count` reaches 3, so `Count` is never shown as 4

> **Exam Hint**
> - Before you write anything in the table, find the statement that ends the loop and predict how many times it will run, then check your table matches

## Tracing loops, arrays and functions

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_P9kBrfg8bk36kw9Y`

## Tracing loops, arrays and functions

### What changes when the loop is a WHILE or REPEAT loop?

- A **WHILE** loop checks its condition **before** each iteration, so the loop body may never run at all
- A **REPEAT ... UNTIL** loop checks its condition **after** each iteration, so the body always runs at least once
- When the condition ends the loop, nothing changes, so **no new row is needed** just for the check
- With **input values** (for example "12, 24, 57, ... 0"), use each value once, in order, and stop when the loop ends, even if values are left over

### Tracing nested loops

- The inner loop runs **completely** for every single iteration of the outer loop
- Write both counters as columns and update the inner counter on every row
- The outer counter only changes when the inner loop has finished

### Tracing arrays

- Each array element in the table gets **its own column**, such as `Mix[1]` to `Mix[4]`
- When the index is a variable, work out the index **first**, then find the element

  - If `Index` is 3, `Mix[Index] ← Mix[Index] - 1` changes `Mix[3]` only
- An element keeps its value until the code changes it, so look back up the column for its latest value

### Tracing functions and string handling

- Use the **Insert** to check exactly what each built-in function returns; the [Paper 2 guide](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/paper-guides/paper-2-problem-solving-and-programming/) explains how to use it

  - `MID("X3Y2W4", 3, 1)` returns `"Y"`, the 1 character starting at position 3
  - `LEFT(Result, 3)` returns the first 3 characters of `Result`
  - `STR_TO_NUM("3")` returns the number 3, not the string "3"
- Keep data types consistent with the question: strings in quotation marks, characters in single quotes, numbers without quotes

  - The **OUTPUT** column is different: write output exactly as it is displayed, without quotation marks
- When a function is called, trace its parameters as the values passed in, and write the **returned value** in the column of the variable that receives it

## Common mistakes in trace tables

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_4M8K3phHgPzQrwtX`

## Common mistakes in trace tables

- Examiner reports for 9618 identify these mistakes:

  - **Missing the initial values**: one series' report noted that otherwise good answers "missed the initial values", which is a full mark lost
  - **Merging iterations**: the same report stressed that students must "keep the values of variables distinct for each iteration of the loop"
  - **Quotation marks around output**: in assembly language traces in Paper 1, otherwise correct tables lost marks for putting quotation marks around the output
  - **Missing the final value**: examiners noted answers that left out the final value of a loop counter (`Index` = 11) after a conditional loop ended
- Other mistakes that cost marks:

  - Running a loop one time too many or one time too few (an **off-by-one error**), often by checking the loop condition with old values
  - Using `/` and `DIV` interchangeably: `DIV` gives the whole-number part only, so `583 DIV 10` is 58

> **Worked Example**
> The procedure `Process()` is written in pseudocode:
> 
> Complete the trace table by dry running the procedure when it is called as follows:
> 
> `CALL Process(5837)`
> 
> **[5]**
> 
> **Answer**:
> 
> | Num | Digit | Total | Count | OUTPUT |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | 5837 |   | 0 | 0 |   |
> | 583 | 7 |   | 1 |   |
> | 58 | 3 |   | 2 |   |
> | 5 | 8 | 8 |   |   |
> | 0 | 5 |   | 3 |   |
> |   |   |   |   | Even total: 8, odd digits: 3 |
> 
> One mark for each of:
> 
> - the initialisation row **[1 mark]**
> - the first two iterations **[1 mark]**
> - the third iteration **[1 mark]**
> - the fourth iteration, with `Num` reaching 0 **[1 mark]**
> - the output **[1 mark]**
> 
> `MOD 10` takes the last digit and `DIV 10` removes it, so the digits are processed from right to left: 7, 3, 8, 5. The loop ends when `Num` is 0, so there is no fifth iteration. See [Writing Pseudocode in the Exam](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/key-exam-skills/writing-pseudocode-in-the-exam/) for how `MOD` and `DIV` work.

> **Exam Hint**
> - When you finish, run your eye down each column: a variable should only change on rows where the code actually assigns it a new value

title: Writing Pseudocode in the Exam
bodyMd:
# Writing Pseudocode in the Exam

## Why Cambridge pseudocode matters

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_gNwTnjwvWBmmGq37`

## Why Cambridge pseudocode matters

### What is Cambridge pseudocode?

- **Cambridge pseudocode** is the standard way of writing algorithms in 9618 exams
- Its rules are set out in the **Pseudocode Guide for Teachers**, published by Cambridge for each syllabus period
- Questions in **Paper 2** and **Paper 3** ask for answers in pseudocode, and any pseudocode printed in those papers is written in this style (Paper 3 also prints assembly language and declarative code, which follow their own rules)
- Examiners state that following the recommended pseudocode lets them **follow the structure and logic** of an answer and credit it; answers written in a programming language are not accepted when a question asks for pseudocode
- For how to work through Paper 2 itself, including using the Insert, see the [Paper 2 guide](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/paper-guides/paper-2-problem-solving-and-programming/)

### Why do Python users lose marks?

- Most students practise programming in Python (or Java or Visual Basic) for Paper 4
- Examiners warn that the syntax of the language you have studied **is not acceptable** in a pseudocode answer
- The table shows the most common Python habits and the Cambridge equivalent

| Python habit | Cambridge pseudocode |
|---|---|
| `x = 5` | `X ← 5` |
| `if x == 5:` | `IF X = 5 THEN` |
| `!=` | `<>` |
| `elif` | no `ELSEIF`: use a nested `IF` inside `ELSE`, or a `CASE` statement |
| `"Hi " + name` | `"Hi " & Name` |
| `//` and `%` | `DIV` and `MOD` |
| `for i in range(1, 11):` | `FOR Index ← 1 TO 10` ... `NEXT Index` |
| `for item in items:` | no equivalent: loop through the index with a `FOR` loop |
| `len(s)`, `s.upper()` | `LENGTH(S)`, `TO_UPPER(S)` (from the Insert) |
| `print()` and `input()` | `OUTPUT` and `INPUT` |
| `return` inside `def` | `RETURN` inside `FUNCTION ... RETURNS <data type>` |
| `# comment` | `// comment` |

- For changing case, use `TO_UPPER` and `TO_LOWER` from the Insert; the Pseudocode Guide lists `UCASE` and `LCASE` instead, but the Insert is what you have in the exam, so use its function names

## Conventions examiners check

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_vFp8Gkqnpk5YsFPv`

## Conventions examiners check

### How do you set out pseudocode?

- **Keywords** are in upper case: `IF`, `WHILE`, `PROCEDURE`
- **Identifiers** (names of variables, constants and modules) are in mixed case, such as `NumberOfPlayers`

  - They may only contain letters, digits and underscores, and must start with a letter
  - They must **never be keywords**, so `String`, `Input` and `Integer` are not valid names
  - They are not case sensitive, so `Total` and `TOTAL` are the same identifier
- Indent the contents of every `IF`, loop and module (usually by three spaces)
- Comments start with `//`

### Declarations and assignment

- Declare each variable with its data type: `INTEGER`, `REAL`, `CHAR`, `STRING`, `BOOLEAN` or `DATE`
- Constants use `=` and can only be given a *literal value*
- Arrays use **square brackets** and state the lower and upper bound
- Assignment always uses the arrow `←`; the `=` sign is only for comparison (and constants)
- On Paper 3, define user-defined types with `TYPE`: a record with `TYPE ... ENDTYPE`, and an enumerated type with `TYPE Season = (Spring, Summer, ...)`; examiners report students using `ENUM` or `DECLARE` where `TYPE` was needed

- String values go in double quotes (`"Ali"`) and single characters in single quotes (`'A'`)
- To access a field of a record stored in an array, put the index on the **array**, then use dot notation: `Batch[Index].Weight`

### Operators

- Arithmetic: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `DIV` (whole-number quotient) and `MOD` (remainder)

  - `/` always gives a `REAL` result, even if both values are integers
- Comparison: `=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`
- Logic: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`; each side of `AND` and `OR` must be a complete condition
- Concatenation: `&`
- Use brackets to make the order of operations clear

### Selection

- Every `IF` needs `THEN` and a matching `ENDIF`
- `CASE` clauses are checked **in order**, and only the first one that matches runs; `OTHERWISE` must come last
- A `CASE` clause can test a range, such as `1 TO 10 : ...`

### Iteration

- `FOR` loops include the `←` and repeat the loop variable after `NEXT`; add `STEP` to count in steps other than 1 (including negative steps)
- `REPEAT ... UNTIL` always runs **at least once**
- `WHILE ... ENDWHILE` may run **zero times**, because the condition is tested first

### Procedures and functions

- A **procedure** is called with `CALL`, as a statement on its own
- A **function** is **never** called with `CALL`; it is used inside an expression, such as an assignment, an `IF` condition or an `OUTPUT`
- When you call a module, write only its name and the values, not the full header with data types
- Parameters are passed **by value** unless `BYREF` is written before them; once written, `BYREF` also applies to the parameters that follow it in the same header

### File handling

- Open a file in `READ`, `WRITE` or `APPEND` mode before using it; `WRITE` creates a new file and wipes any existing data
- Use `READFILE` and `WRITEFILE` (not `READ` or `WRITE` on their own) and close every file with `CLOSEFILE`
- The file name must be in **quotes** when it is written directly, and must be included in `EOF()` and `CLOSEFILE`

## Mistakes that cost marks

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_jXybnp3BGRphTpcm`

## Mistakes that cost marks

### Which pseudocode errors do examiners see most?

- Cambridge examiner reports list invalid pseudocode like the examples below; each one loses marks

| What students wrote | What is wrong | Correct pseudocode |
|---|---|---|
| `FOR X 1 TO 100` | The assignment arrow is missing | `FOR X ← 1 TO 100` |
| `FOR Index ← 1 TO EOF(Filename)` | `EOF` returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`, not a number of lines | `WHILE NOT EOF(Filename)` |
| `IF X = 3 OR 4 OR 5 THEN` | Each side of `OR` must be a full comparison | `IF X = 3 OR X = 4 OR X = 5 THEN` |
| `WHILE Number >= 100 AND <= 200` | The second condition has no left-hand side | `WHILE Number >= 100 AND Number <= 200` |
| `IF Num ← 43 THEN` | `←` assigns a value; it does not compare | `IF Num = 43 THEN` |
| `DECLARE String : STRING` | A keyword is used as an identifier | `DECLARE UserName : STRING` |
| `CALL Valid(MyString)` then `IF RESULT = TRUE THEN` | Functions are not called with `CALL`, and `RESULT` does not exist | `IF Valid(MyString) = TRUE THEN` |
| `Batch.Weight(Index)` | The index belongs to the array of records, in square brackets | `Batch[Index].Weight` |
| `OPENFILE Stock.txt FOR READ` | A file name written directly needs quotes | `OPENFILE "Stock.txt" FOR READ` |
| `OUTPUT "Total: " & Total` (where `Total` is an `INTEGER`) | `&` only joins strings, so an integer must be converted or separated with a comma | `OUTPUT "Total: ", Total` or `OUTPUT "Total: " & NUM_TO_STR(Total)` |
| `FOR WebName in Secret` | This is programming language syntax | Loop through the indexes with `FOR Index ← 1 TO ...` |

- To practise finding and correcting errors like these in a given algorithm, see [Test Data & Finding Errors](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/key-exam-skills/test-data-and-finding-errors/)

### Missing end statements

- Examiners report that many marks are lost through small omissions, such as:

  - a correct procedure or function header with no `ENDPROCEDURE` or `ENDFUNCTION`
  - an `IF` with no `ENDIF`
  - a loop with no `ENDWHILE`, `UNTIL` or `NEXT`

> **Worked Example**
> A global 1D array `Marks` stores the test marks of 30 students. The lower bound of the array is 1.
> 
> A student was asked to write pseudocode for a function `Average()` that returns the mean of the marks in `Marks`. This is their answer:
> 
> Rewrite the answer as valid Cambridge pseudocode.
> 
> **[5]**
> 
> **Answer**:
> 
> - Function header with `RETURNS REAL`, and `ENDFUNCTION` **[1 mark]**
> - Declare and initialise `Total` using `←` **[1 mark]**
> - `FOR` loop from 1 to 30 with `NEXT Index` **[1 mark]**
> - Add each element to `Total` using `←` inside the loop **[1 mark]**
> - `RETURN` the total divided by 30** [1 mark]**
> 
> - `range(30)` counts from 0 to 29, so with a lower bound of 1 it would try to read `Marks[0]`, which does not exist, and would miss `Marks[30]`
> - `print` outputs the value instead of returning it to the calling code

> **Exam Hint**
> - Write the closing keyword (`ENDIF`, `NEXT`, `ENDWHILE`, `ENDFUNCTION`) straight after the opening line, then fill in the body, so you never lose a mark for a missing end statement
> - In a function, finish with `RETURN`, not `OUTPUT`: examiners regularly see `OUTPUT` used where the value should be returned, and it does not gain the mark

title: Paper 1: Theory Fundamentals
bodyMd:
# Paper 1: Theory Fundamentals

## Paper 1 overview

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_pfN4szScSmvDjSDN`

## Paper 1 overview

### What is in 9618 Paper 1?

- Paper 1 Theory Fundamentals is a **1 hour 30 minute written paper** worth **75 marks**
- It is **50% of the AS Level** and **25% of the A Level**
- It covers syllabus sections 1 to 8:

  - information representation
  - communication
  - hardware
  - processor fundamentals
  - system software
  - security, privacy and data integrity
  - ethics and ownership
  - databases
- You answer **all** questions; there is no choice
- **Calculators are not allowed**, so every conversion and file size calculation is done by hand
- Questions range from 1-mark recall to longer answers set in a scenario, such as a company, a device or a network
- For advice that applies to every 9618 paper, see:

  - [CIE A Level Computer Science exam tips](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/exam-technique/exam-tips/)
  - [9618 command words](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/exam-technique/command-words/)

## Question types and how to answer them

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_kC6s9Jfz2CmDRGD2`

## Question types and how to answer them

### How do you answer number conversion questions?

- Typical stems include:

  - "Convert the denary number 241 to hexadecimal"
  - "Convert the two's complement binary number into denary"
  - "Subtract the denary number 10 from the denary number 100 using binary subtraction. Show your working."
- Check **which representation** the question gives you before you start

  - Examiners reported a very common wrong answer where students treated an unsigned binary integer as **Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)** and converted it directly
  - Another common error was converting a binary integer into **denary** when the question asked for **hexadecimal**
- If the question says "using binary subtraction" (or binary addition), the working **must be in binary**

  - Examiners give **no credit** for doing the calculation in denary and converting the answer to binary
  - Watch the order: 100 − 10 is not the same as 10 − 100, and examiners report this being reversed

### How do you answer file size calculations?

- Typical stems include:

  - "Calculate the file size of a bitmap image... Give your answer in kibibytes. Show your working."
  - "Calculate the file size of the recording. Give your answer in megabytes and show your working."
- Mark schemes usually award **1 mark for the working** and **1 mark for the answer**
- Follow three steps:

  - Multiply the values given (for an image: width × height × bit depth)
  - **Divide by 8** if the bit depth is in bits and the answer is in bytes; examiners report that a frequent wrong answer **missed this division**
  - Divide by 1000 or 1024 for each step up in units, depending on which unit the question asks for
- Check the unit the question asks for, as the decimal and binary prefixes are different

| Decimal unit | Size | Binary unit | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| kilobyte (kB) | 1000 bytes | kibibyte (KiB) | 1024 bytes |
| megabyte (MB) | 1000 kB | mebibyte (MiB) | 1024 KiB |
| gigabyte (GB) | 1000 MB | gibibyte (GiB) | 1024 MiB |

- Examiners also report students confusing these units, for example swapping kibibytes and kilobytes
- Without a calculator, choose an order of working that keeps the numbers simple; for example, divide by 8 and by 1024 early when the values are powers of 2

### How do you answer bit depth, resolution and sampling questions?

- These questions usually ask about the **effect** of a change, not the definition
- Say clearly **whether the value increases or decreases**, then describe the effect on the image or the sound
- Examiners report that many answers about changing bit depth only talked about **file size** when the question asked how the **image** is affected
- Restating the definition ("increasing the bit depth increases the number of bits per pixel") is not enough; say what changes for the user, such as more colours being available

### How do you answer logic gate and truth table questions?

- Typical stems include "Draw the logic circuit for the logic expression" and "Complete the truth table for the logic expression"
- Draw each gate with the **correct shape**

  - Examiners report that OR and AND gates were often hard to tell apart, and that NOT gates were drawn **without the circle**
- Draw the circuit **exactly as the expression is written**

  - Examiners report missing NOT gates, and students replacing (NOT R) OR (NOT M) with a single NOR gate, which is a different expression
- In a truth table, list the inputs in binary counting order (000, 001, 010...) so that no row is missed

### How do you answer questions set in a scenario?

- Many Paper 1 questions describe a situation, such as a video doorbell, a laser printer or a company network, then ask you to describe or explain something about it
- Every point should link to the scenario; a textbook definition on its own often scores nothing
- For 2-mark questions, give **two different points**; examiners report answers where the same point was written twice in different words. If the answer space is numbered, only the first answer in each space is marked
- Read the scenario details carefully, as they often tell you which answer is expected (for example, a question about a bitmap image needs an answer about pixels and colours, not about text characters)

### How do you answer ethics and ownership questions?

- Typical stems include "Explain the reasons why the computer programmer needs to act ethically towards colleagues" and "Explain why it is important for a programmer to join a professional ethical body"
- Learn what a ***professional ethical body*** is (the syllabus names the British Computer Society (BCS) and the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE)); examiners report students thinking it was an employer or part of the company
- When a scenario describes someone acting unethically, explain **why** their action was unethical; examiners report that answers only saying what the person *should* have done did not answer the question

### How do you answer assembly language trace questions?

- Typical stems ask you to complete a trace table showing the contents of the Accumulator (ACC), the Index Register (IX) and memory as each instruction runs
- Work through one instruction at a time and update only the register or memory location that the instruction changes
- Examiners report three common errors:

  - **Indexed addressing** is often misunderstood; for example, `LDX 110` was wrongly treated as loading the value 110 into the accumulator
  - Storing a value from the accumulator **copies** it; the accumulator is **not** reset to zero
  - Output values are written without quotation marks; otherwise correct trace tables lost marks for putting the output in quotation marks

### How do you answer SQL questions?

- Typical stems include "Write a Structured Query Language (SQL) script to..." and "Write a Data Definition Language (DDL) script to..."
- Copy table and attribute names exactly as the question gives them; examiners report marks lost when these were copied wrongly
- If a question asks you to identify and correct errors in an SQL script, write the corrected statement as well as naming the error; examiners report answers that found the errors but gave no correction
- Use SQL data types such as `VARCHAR(n)`, `INTEGER` and `DATE`, not data types from a programming language
- Put quotation marks around text values but not around Boolean or numeric values, and use the SQL functions in the syllabus, such as `AVG`, `SUM` and `COUNT`; examiners report marks lost for quotation marks around a Boolean value in a `WHERE` clause
- Examiners report that the primary and foreign key clauses are often the hardest part, so learn `PRIMARY KEY (Field)` and `FOREIGN KEY (Field) REFERENCES Table (Field)`

## Common mistakes in Paper 1

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_yZvfddG8jCC6NRcz`

## Common mistakes in Paper 1

- Answering in denary when the question asks for hexadecimal, or the other way round
- Leaving out the "divide by 8" step in file size calculations
- Not stating whether a value goes up or down when describing the effect of a change
- Replacing a combination of gates with a single NOR gate, which changes the expression
- Writing the same point twice in different words for a 2-mark question

> **Worked Example**
> A bitmap image has a resolution of 1024 pixels wide and 512 pixels high. The bit depth is 24 bits.
> 
> Calculate the file size of the image. Give your answer in kibibytes. Show your working.
> 
> **[2]**
> 
> **Answer**:
> 
> Working: (1024 × 512 × 24) / 8 / 1024 **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answer: 1536 KiB **[1 mark]**
> 
> Dividing by 8 converts bits to bytes and dividing by 1024 converts bytes to kibibytes; dividing by 1024 first gives 512 × 24 / 8 = 512 × 3 = 1536, which is easy to work out without a calculator.

> **Exam Hint**
> - Before answering a conversion or file size question, underline the unit or number base the answer must be in, because a correct value in the wrong form loses the mark
> - When a question says "using binary subtraction" or "show your working", the working itself carries marks, so set it out in full even if you can do it in your head

title: Paper 2: Problem-solving and Programming
bodyMd:
# Paper 2: Problem-solving and Programming

## Paper 2 overview

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_zZrvwv5Vp3nHcGtj`

## Paper 2 overview

### What is in Paper 2?

- Paper 2 is **Fundamental Problem-solving and Programming Skills**
- It is a **2-hour written paper worth 75 marks**: 50% of the AS Level and 25% of the A Level
- It assesses syllabus sections 9 to 12: algorithm design, data types and structures, programming, and software development
- Most marks (60%) are for **designing and writing solutions** (assessment objective 3, AO3), with the rest (40%, AO2) for applying knowledge to a scenario; there are no marks for straight recall
- Answers that involve code must be written in **Cambridge pseudocode**, not in a programming language
- An **Insert** is provided with the paper, listing the built-in functions and operators you may use
- Calculators are not allowed

### How is Paper 2 different from Paper 4?

- Both papers test programming, but in different ways

| Feature | Paper 2 | Paper 4 |
|---|---|---|
| Where | On paper | On a computer, with no internet |
| Language | Cambridge pseudocode only | Java, Visual Basic or Python (console mode) |
| Level | AS Level (and part of the A Level) | A Level only |
| Code checked by | An examiner reading your pseudocode | An examiner reading your copied code and test evidence |
| Built-in functions | Only those listed in the Insert | Those of your chosen language |

- Examiners warn that students who practise in a programming language for Paper 4 often carry its syntax into Paper 2, which loses marks; see [Writing Pseudocode in the Exam](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/key-exam-skills/writing-pseudocode-in-the-exam/)

## Using the Insert

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_zjk5YF9GZFd27Nkb`

## Using the Insert

### What is in the Insert?

- The Insert is a separate booklet that lists every built-in pseudocode function and operator you can use in your answers, with an example of each

  - **String functions**: `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `MID`, `LENGTH`, `TO_UPPER`, `TO_LOWER`, `NUM_TO_STR`, `STR_TO_NUM`, `IS_NUM`, `ASC`, `CHR`
  - **Numeric functions**: `INT`, `RAND`
  - **Date functions**: `DAY`, `MONTH`, `YEAR`, `DAYINDEX`, `SETDATE`, `TODAY`
  - **Text file function**: `EOF`
  - **Operators**: `&` (concatenation), `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, `MOD`, `DIV` and the comparison operators
- Some questions tell you to use a function from the Insert, for example "Date functions from the insert should be used in your solution"

### How should you use the Insert?

- **Only use functions that are in the Insert**: examiners state that language-specific functions or methods that are not in it will not gain credit
- If the Insert and the Pseudocode Guide use different names for the same function, use the Insert's name; for example, use `TO_UPPER` from the Insert rather than `UCASE` from the Guide
- Check the **parameter order and return type** before you use a function; for example, `MID(ThisString, x, y)` returns `y` characters starting at position `x`
- Use the date functions when a question involves dates; in one recent series many students lost marks for not using the correct date function from the Insert to assign a date
- You may annotate the Insert and plan on it, but answers written on the Insert are not marked

## Question types in Paper 2

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_Pgp6GZDW95KywxNb`

## Question types in Paper 2

### What kinds of question come up?

- Every Paper 2 has questions that ask you to **write pseudocode**; most also include several of the types below

### Short questions on the Insert and data types

- Most Paper 2s open with short tables: give the data type of a variable or an example value, or evaluate an expression that uses Insert functions, such as `MID(CharList, MONTH(FlagDay), 1)`

### Writing a module

- The most valuable questions ask you to write a whole **procedure or function** from a description, often worth 6 to 8 marks
- The description is usually a table with a bullet point for each thing the module must do; these bullets are the basis of the mark scheme (see "How to plan a 6 to 8 mark algorithm question")

### Describing an algorithm in steps

- Some questions ask you to describe the steps of an algorithm without writing the code, for example "Describe the steps that the algorithm should perform. Do not include pseudocode statements in your answer."
- Write numbered steps that each do **one thing** (initialise a total, start a loop, input a value, test it, update the total, output the result)
- Examiners report vague steps that deal with all the values at once (such as "find all marks less than 20"); describe what happens to one value at a time inside a loop

### Completing or correcting code

- You may be given pseudocode with **gaps to fill** or **errors to find and correct**
- When correcting errors, write the original line and the corrected line, both clearly labelled; examiners describe this as the clearest way to answer, and adding the line number makes it clearer still
- See [Test Data and Finding Errors](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/key-exam-skills/test-data-and-finding-errors/) for how to spot each type of error

### Trace tables and dry runs

- You may be asked to *dry run* an algorithm and complete a trace table
- See [Trace Tables](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/key-exam-skills/trace-tables/) for the step-by-step method

### Design diagrams

- Structure charts appear in more than half of the Paper 2s set from 2021 to 2024 (12 of 21); you may be asked to draw one or to complete one with modules, parameters and the direction they are passed
- Examiners report marks lost for missing parameter labels, for not shading the arrow of a Boolean parameter, and for leaving out the selection diamond when one module calls either one module or another
- **Program flowcharts** come up often, either to draw from pseudocode or to convert into pseudocode
- **State-transition diagrams** appear less often (6 of the 21 papers); you are usually asked to complete a table of inputs, outputs and next states from a diagram, or to complete the diagram from a table

### Data structures and files

- Questions on **stacks, queues and linked lists** usually ask how they are **implemented using arrays and pointers**, not just how they behave

  - Examiners noted that many students missed the word "implemented" in one question and described a linked list in general terms, scoring few marks
- Most Paper 2s include **text file handling**, such as reading every line of a file or writing results to a new file

## How to plan a 6 to 8 mark algorithm question

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_6NZzQgKB3GQvVM82`

## How to plan a 6 to 8 mark algorithm question

### How are algorithm questions marked?

- Algorithm questions are marked **per feature**, not as all-or-nothing
- The mark scheme lists **mark points**, and each one is awarded if your pseudocode does that thing, even if other parts are wrong
- For example, in a recent 8-mark question to write a procedure that checks candidates' marks and writes some IDs to a file, the mark points included:

  - the procedure heading, parameter and ending
  - opening the file in **write** mode and closing it
  - a loop through all the candidates
  - calling the given function with the candidate's mark as the parameter
  - incrementing a count when the function returns `TRUE`
  - writing the ID to the file after converting it to a string
  - outputting the count **after** the loop

### Step-by-step method

1. **Underline each requirement** in the question or the module description table; each bullet usually maps to one or more mark points
2. **Write the header first**: `PROCEDURE` or `FUNCTION`, the identifier, the parameters with data types and, for a function, `RETURNS` and the data type
3. **Declare and initialise** the variables you need, such as a count set to 0
4. **Choose the loop**: `FOR` when you know how many times (for example, the size of an array), `WHILE NOT EOF(...)` for reading a file of unknown length
5. **Write the body** one requirement at a time, ticking each underlined bullet as you cover it
6. **Finish** by closing any file, then add the output or `RETURN` and the end statement (`ENDPROCEDURE` or `ENDFUNCTION`); nothing after `RETURN` is executed
7. **Check** that you have used the identifier names given in the question, not your own versions; examiners report marks lost for not using the array or variable names stated in the question

### How can you still pick up marks if your code isn't perfect?

- Examiners say in report after report that even the hardest pseudocode questions **contain accessible marks**
- If you cannot see the whole solution, still write:

  - the header and end statement
  - the variable declarations and initialisation
  - the loop structure
  - the file open and close
  - the final `RETURN` or `OUTPUT`
- Do not add things the question did not ask for, such as storing every input in an array; they gain nothing and take time

> **Worked Example**
> A text file `Scores.txt` stores one test score per line as a string. The number of lines in the file is not known.
> 
> A function `CountAbove()` will:
> 
> - take an integer parameter `Threshold`
> - read each score from the file
> - count how many scores are greater than `Threshold`
> - return the count
> 
> Write pseudocode for the function `CountAbove()`.
> 
> **[6]**
> 
> **Answer**:
> 
> - Function header with the parameter, `RETURNS INTEGER` and `ENDFUNCTION` **[1 mark]**
> - Open the file in `READ` mode and close it after the loop **[1 mark]**
> - Conditional loop that ends when `EOF` is reached **[1 mark]**
> - Read a line from the file inside the loop **[1 mark]**
> - Convert the line to a number and compare it with `Threshold`, incrementing `Count` if it is greater **[1 mark]**
> - Initialise `Count` to 0 before the loop and return it after the loop **[1 mark]**
> 
> Each bullet in the description maps to at least one mark point, so a student who could not work out the comparison would still score 5 out of 6.

> **Exam Hint**
> - If a question asks for a function, end with `RETURN`, not `OUTPUT`; examiners regularly see `OUTPUT` used where the value should be returned
> - If your answer runs out of space, continue on an additional page and write the question number clearly, rather than squeezing pseudocode into the margins where the examiner may not be able to read it

title: Paper 3: Advanced Theory
bodyMd:
# Paper 3: Advanced Theory

## Paper 3 overview

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_gKhFm7x3R2GddbCP`

## Paper 3 overview

### What is in Paper 3?

- Paper 3 Advanced Theory is a **1 hour 30 minute written paper** worth **75 marks**
- It is **25% of the A Level** and is only sat by A Level students
- It covers syllabus sections 13 to 20:

  - data representation (including floating-point numbers)
  - communication and internet technologies
  - hardware and virtual machines (including Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps)
  - system software (including Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) and Backus-Naur Form (BNF))
  - security
  - artificial intelligence
  - computational thinking and problem-solving
  - further programming
- You answer **all** questions, and **calculators are not allowed**
- Many questions are **multi-step methods** where the working earns marks; examiner reports remind students that if a question asks for working, it must be shown to gain full credit
- Questions that need pseudocode must follow the Cambridge pseudocode guide
- For general 9618 advice and the Paper 1 skills that Paper 3 builds on, see:

  - [CIE A Level Computer Science exam tips](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/exam-technique/exam-tips/)
  - [9618 command words](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/exam-technique/command-words/)
  - [Writing Cambridge pseudocode in the exam](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/key-exam-skills/writing-pseudocode-in-the-exam/)
  - [How to answer Paper 1: Theory Fundamentals](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/computer-science/cie/19/revision-notes/21-exam-skills/paper-guides/paper-1-theory-fundamentals/)

## Question types and how to answer them

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_3P5cYc3rF8fgX8m9`

## Question types and how to answer them

### How do you answer floating-point questions?

- Typical stems include:

  - "Calculate the normalised floating-point representation of +54.8125 in this system. Show your working."
  - "Calculate the denary value of the given normalised binary floating-point number"
- The system is given in the question; for example, **12 bits for the mantissa and 4 bits for the exponent**, both in **two's complement**
- Mark schemes credit each stage separately:

  - converting the number to binary
  - working out the exponent (how many places the binary point moves)
  - the correct final mantissa and exponent
- Examiners report students losing marks on the exponent: errors in calculating it, or not showing how it was worked out and applied to the mantissa
- Check that the result is normalised: a positive mantissa starts `01` and a negative mantissa starts `10`
- Fill **every bit** of the mantissa and exponent, padding with zeros where needed
- For questions about range or precision, link the bits to the effect: more mantissa bits give greater precision and more exponent bits give a greater range; examiners credited answers that said how many bits the mantissa had, why that was too few, and that precision would be lost

### How do you answer Boolean algebra and Karnaugh map questions?

- Typical stems include:

  - "Write the Boolean expression that corresponds to the logic circuit as a sum-of-products"
  - "Complete the Karnaugh map (K-map) for the given truth table"
  - "Draw loop(s) around appropriate group(s) in the K-map to produce an optimal sum-of-products"
- **Fill every cell** of a K-map with a 0 or a 1; examiners only award marks for a complete map using 0s and 1s
- Loops must contain 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells and can wrap around the edges; use the **largest** groups possible
- Give the answer in the form asked for

  - If the question asks for a **sum-of-products**, do not simplify it further; examiners report many wrong answers that gave simplified expressions the question did not ask for
  - If the question asks you to simplify, **show all the stages** and name the law used where you can
  - When you apply De Morgan's laws, change the operator as well as splitting the bar: NOT (A AND B) becomes (NOT A) OR (NOT B); examiners report answers that split the bar but left AND as AND

### How do you answer Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) questions?

- Typical stems include:

  - "Evaluate this RPN expression"
  - "Show the changing contents of the stack as the RPN expression is evaluated"
  - Converting between infix and RPN
- When showing the stack during RPN evaluation, only operands go on the stack; examiners report a common error of putting the **operators** on the stack
- Show the stack after **every** push and pop, not only the final value
- When converting RPN to infix, **include brackets**; examiners report that leaving them out changes the order of operations and makes the answer wrong

### How do you answer BNF and syntax diagram questions?

- Typical stems include "Complete the Backus-Naur Form (BNF) for the given syntax diagrams" and "Draw a syntax diagram for..."
- Use exact BNF notation: `<name>` for each *non-terminal*, `::=` for "is defined as" and `|` between alternatives
- Examiners report that students often understood the syntax diagram but lost marks for **BNF that was not fully correct**
- For recursion (for example, a code made of one or more digits), define the item in terms of itself, such as `<code> ::= <digit> | <digit><code>`

### How do you answer graph algorithm questions?

- Typical stems include "Calculate the shortest distance between the base and each of the other towns in the diagram using Dijkstra's algorithm" and "Describe the purpose of both the A* algorithm and Dijkstra's algorithm"
- For a Dijkstra trace, show the working the examiners look for:

  - set the start node to 0 and every other node to infinity (∞)
  - update each distance as shorter routes are found
  - record which nodes have been visited
- For "purpose" questions, the purpose of both algorithms is to find the **shortest (optimum) path between two nodes**; the A* algorithm also uses a ***heuristic*** to guide the search

### How do you answer declarative programming questions?

- Typical stems describe a set of facts (for example, students and the subjects they choose) and ask you to write extra clauses, or to give the result of a *goal*
- Examiners report that the highest marks went to students who remembered that:

  - **every clause ends with a full stop**
  - **facts use lower-case letters only**
  - clauses are written in the correct order with no spelling errors
- When giving the output of a goal, do not add capital letters or a full stop to the list of results

### How do you answer object-oriented programming questions?

- Typical stems include "Outline the structure of a class", "Give three differences between an object and a class" and writing pseudocode for a class with a constructor
- In pseudocode, close every class with `ENDCLASS`; examiners report that missing `ENDCLASS` was a typical error
- Use **the identifiers already given** in the question for attributes and parameters; examiners report marks lost for using different variable names in declarations or the constructor
- For definitions, be specific: "inheritance is when a new class **derives** attributes and methods from a parent class" scores, where a vague phrase does not

### How do you answer user-defined data type questions?

- Typical stems include "Write pseudocode statements to declare the record data type...", or to declare an enumerated, set or pointer type
- Declare every user-defined type with the keyword `TYPE`; a record type ends with `ENDTYPE`. Examiners report marks lost for starting the definition with `DECLARE`, or for not beginning it with `TYPE`
- Use the type names, field names and data types given in the question

### How do you answer "purpose" questions?

- Some Paper 3 questions ask for the **purpose** of something, such as asymmetric key cryptography or quantum cryptography
- Examiners report that describing **how it works** or listing its features does not answer a purpose question; say **what it is for** and **why it is used**

## Showing working on multi-step questions

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_sSHSh82h7NJV5PpB`

## Showing working on multi-step questions

### What should your working include?

- In Paper 3, the method often earns more marks than the final answer

| Question type | What your working should show |
|---|---|
| Floating-point to binary | The number in binary, the number of places the point moves, then the final mantissa and exponent |
| Floating-point to denary | The exponent in denary, where the point moves to, then the denary value |
| K-map | Every cell filled with 0 or 1, the loops drawn, then one product term per loop |
| Boolean simplification | Every stage of the simplification |
| RPN evaluation | The stack after every push and every operation |
| Dijkstra's algorithm | Starting values (0 and ∞) and each updated distance |

- If you run out of time on a multi-step question, write down the stages you have completed; examiners report that students earned credit for **correct methods** even when the final answer was wrong

> **Worked Example**
> Real numbers are stored in a computer using floating-point representation with:
> 
> - 12 bits for the mantissa
> - 4 bits for the exponent
> - two's complement form for both the mantissa and the exponent
> 
> Calculate the normalised floating-point representation of +27.375 in this system. Show your working.
> 
> **[3]**
> 
> **Answer**:
> 
> - 27.375 converted to binary: 11011.011 **[1 mark]**
> - The binary point moves 5 places to the left to give 0.11011011, so the exponent is 5 **[1 mark]**
> - Mantissa: 011011011000, Exponent: 0101 **[1 mark]**
> 
> The mantissa starts with 01, which shows it is a normalised positive number; the remaining bits are padded with zeros to fill all 12 bits.

> **Exam Hint**
> - Write the exponent as a denary number in your working before converting it to binary, because examiners report marks lost on the exponent step

## Common mistakes in Paper 3

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_xKyzM9cQ92hCFpSK`

## Common mistakes in Paper 3

- Getting the exponent wrong, or not showing how it was calculated, in floating-point questions
- Leaving K-map cells blank or using symbols other than 0 and 1
- Simplifying a sum-of-products when the question did not ask for it
- Putting operators on the stack when evaluating RPN
- Leaving out brackets when converting RPN to infix
- Using capital letters in facts or in the output of a goal, or missing the full stop at the end of a clause
- Describing how something works when the question asks for its purpose

title: Paper 4: Practical
bodyMd:
# Paper 4: Practical

## How the Paper 4 practical exam works

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_W4FPw5fkNDr5FZyd`

## How the Paper 4 practical exam works

### What happens in Paper 4?

- Paper 4 is the **practical programming paper** for Cambridge International A Level Computer Science (9618)
- It lasts **2 hours 30 minutes**, is worth **75 marks** and makes up **25% of the A Level**
- It is taken **on a computer**, with **no internet or email access**
- Programs must be written in one of three languages, in console mode:

  - Java
  - Python
  - Visual Basic
- A mark of zero is given if any other language is used
- All 75 marks are for **assessment objective 3 (AO3): design, programming and evaluation**

### What does a Paper 4 question look like?

- The paper has **three questions**, each built around **one scenario**, such as a queue of jobs, a set of trains and stations or a file of toy records
- The scenario is split into **many small parts**, usually worth 1 to 8 marks each
- Later parts build on earlier ones; for example, you write a class in part (a), use it in the main program in part (b) and extend the main program in part (c)
- Some parts give **pseudocode** or a description of the algorithm to turn into program code; others only describe what the subroutine must do
- You may be given **source files**, such as a text file of data or starter code, to use

## The evidence document

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_xPtjNx65G5JGdV2N`

## The evidence document

### Why does the evidence document matter so much?

- The syllabus is explicit: "If there is no evidence of work in the evidence document, the work will not receive any marks"
- Examiners **only see the evidence document**, not your program files, so a perfect program that is not pasted in scores zero
- Each task tells you which part of the evidence document to paste into, for example "Copy and paste the program code into part 1(b) in the evidence document"

### Program code evidence

- **Copy and paste code as text**, not as a screenshot

  - Examiners report that screenshots of code from an integrated development environment (IDE), especially coloured text on a dark background, are often unreadable and cannot gain marks
- Paste the code into the **correct box** for that question part
- Check that **all of the code is visible**, including the first line of each subroutine and the lines at the right-hand edge of the page
- In Python, check that the **indentation** has survived the paste; examiner reports stress that it must be included and accurate
- If you change code from an earlier part, **update the earlier evidence** as well

### Testing evidence

- When a part says "Test your program", take a **screenshot of the output** and paste it into the named box
- The screenshot must show **every input** as well as the output, so the examiner can check that one produced the other
- Use **black text on a white background**, and make the screenshot large enough to read
- If the output is too long for one screenshot, **use two or more**
- Testing parts are usually worth only 1 or 2 marks each, between 4 and 8 marks per paper in recent series, but they are among the most accessible marks on the paper

## Question types in Paper 4

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_wsHCt8x2VP2RbrnX`

## Question types in Paper 4

### Which topics come up most?

- Paper 4 papers from 2021 to 2026 repeatedly test the same small set of topics:

| Question type | What you are typically asked to write | Marks often given for |
|---|---|---|
| Abstract data types (ADTs): stack, queue, linked list, binary tree | Declare the array and pointers; write `Push()`/`Pop()`, `Enqueue()`/`Dequeue()` or insert and remove routines | Checking for full or empty; updating the pointer; returning the correct value |
| Object-oriented programming (OOP) | Declare a class with private attributes, a constructor and get/set methods; create objects; sometimes inheritance; in Python, declare the attributes using comments when the question asks for it | Correct attribute types; constructor parameters assigned to attributes; methods returning values |
| File handling | Read data from a text file into an array or objects; sometimes write data to a file | Opening the file; looping to the end of the file; storing each line; closing the file; *exception handling* |
| Recursion | Write a recursive subroutine, such as an in-order tree traversal or a recursive search | A base case; a recursive call with a changed parameter; using the returned value |
| Sorting and searching | Write a bubble sort, insertion sort, linear search or binary search on an array | Correct loop limits; the comparison and swap; returning the found index or a "not found" value |

- If you write in Python, include the attribute declarations as comments; every Paper 4 from 2024 to 2026 asks for this, because examiners want to see your declarations and data types even though Python does not need them

### Exception handling

- Many file-handling parts give a mark for **exception handling**, for example `try` and `except` in Python or `try` and `catch` in Java and Visual Basic
- Examiner reports note that some students did not attempt it at all, losing an easy mark
- Put the file-opening and reading statements **inside** the `try` block, and output a suitable message in the `except` or `catch` block

### Turning pseudocode into program code

- When a question gives pseudocode, it is **not written in any one language**, so it may need adapting
- Examiner reports give the example of loop conditions that had to be changed in Python to run the correct number of times

  - The pseudocode `FOR Count ← 1 TO 10` runs 10 times, so in Python it needs `range(1, 11)`, not `range(1, 10)`
- Python also needs the `global` keyword inside a subroutine that assigns a new value to a global variable, such as a pointer
- **Test each subroutine as soon as you write it**, even when the question does not ask for a screenshot

## How to manage your time in Paper 4

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_6XQf9yqqt8DdKdmY`

## How to manage your time in Paper 4

### How long should each part take?

- With 150 minutes for 75 marks, you have about **2 minutes per mark**

  - A 6-mark subroutine is worth about 12 minutes
  - A 1-mark test screenshot should take about 2 minutes
- Spend the first few minutes **reading each whole question**, including all its parts, before you write any code

  - Examiner reports point out that knowing the later parts can change how you write the earlier ones
- Save your work regularly using the file names given in the question

### What if you get stuck on one part?

- **Move on and attempt the later parts**: they are often marked independently
- Examiner reports describe students gaining marks for calling a subroutine in the main program even though they had not managed to write the subroutine
- Leave yourself time at the end to **check the evidence document** against every "Copy and paste" instruction in the paper

## Common mistakes in Paper 4

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_HrfrgxY9QVk5pKYz`

## Common mistakes in Paper 4

- These mistakes appear repeatedly in Cambridge examiner reports for Paper 4:

  - Mixing up **parameters** and **inputs**: taking a value as an input when the question says it is passed as a parameter, or the other way round
  - Calling a function but **not storing or using the value it returns**, when the question asks for the return value to be output
  - Using extra arrays when the question asks for a single array, so the solution **does not meet the requirements** given
  - Leaving out the **constructor parameters** that the question specifies for a class, or writing get methods that take a parameter or output a value instead of returning it
  - Submitting files other than the evidence document, or a zipped evidence document

> **Worked Example**
> A program uses a stack to store integers. The stack is stored in the global 1D array `Stack`, which has space for 5 integers. The global variable `TopPointer` stores the index of the top item in the stack and is initialised to −1. Each element of `Stack` is initialised to −1.
> 
> The function `Push()` takes an integer as a parameter. If the stack is full, the function returns `FALSE`. Otherwise, it adds the integer to the top of the stack and returns `TRUE`.
> 
> (a) Write program code for `Push()`.
> 
> **[4]**
